Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
If M is complete, then for any sequence \((F_n)\) of nonempty closed sets satisfying \(F_{n+1}\subset F_n\) and \(\operatorname{diam} F_n\rightarrow0\), the selected points \(x_n\in F_n\) satisfy \(d(x_m,x_n)\le \operatorname{diam} F_n\) for \(m\ge n\).
Does completeness then force \((x_n)\) to converge to some \(x\)?
Every \(F_n\) is closed and contains the entire tail \(x_m\) with \(m\ge n\), so every \(F_n\) contains the limit \(x\).
In the converse case, every Cauchy sequence \((y_n)\) produces nested nonempty closed tails \(F_n=\overline{\{y_m:m\ge n\}}\) with \(\operatorname{diam} F_n\rightarrow0\).
Does the assumed property then place some \(x\) in all \(F_n\)?
The inequality \(d(y_m,x)\le \operatorname{diam} F_m\) for every \(m\) then gives convergence to \(x\) and proves completeness.
